projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Ellis Barklow was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Today is May 15, 2004. This is the beginning of an interview with Ellis Barklow at his home at 1726 Flamingo Avenue in Chico, California. Mr. Barklow is 78-years-old and had been born on September 18, 1923. My name a Karl Arnet and the other interviewer is Patrick Green and we will be interviewing Ellis Barklow. Ellis Barklow is Kyle's grandfather and his mother's stepfather.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: I'm sorry. I didn't get your name, I don't have it.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: First name is Ellis.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Ellis?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Ellis.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Ellis?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Barklow.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: All right, PJ. Is it all right if I call you Ellis or would you like me to call you Mr. Barklow or --

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Would you like me to call you, Mr. Barklow?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: No. Call me Ellis.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Is it turned on? What branch did you serve in?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Navy.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: How did you chose the Navy over like the Air force, the Army or --

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: I just didn't want to sleep in a trench. I thought, you know, the Navy had bunk beds, you know.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: I thought it would be a little cleaner. I just -- my thoughts on it. I always said that, "Boy, I can't see digging a trench or a fox hole and crawling into it."

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: A little nicer quarters, conditions?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Were you drafted or did you sign up?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: No. I enlisted at 17.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: What year was that?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: 1944. I graduated from high school in June and I went in the -- in the Navy that September.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: September?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Was there any reason in particular that you joined the Navy instead of going into like college or work or anything?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Well, there was a war on, World War II. And it was either being drafted into the Army when I turned 18 or at 17, with your parent's consent, you could enlist in the Navy and sign up and join that way and that's what I did before I turned 18. I signed up at 17 and joined. So when I turned 18 they couldn't draft me.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: That way you could do what you wish to do?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah, righ.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: That makes sense. So you were 17 when you enlisted in 1944 and was it pretty tough? The whole like training and --

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Oh, it was. You know, I was just a kid. You know, out of school and I was nieve about everything and you get thrown in there with a bunch of older guys. There were several of us that were my age but there was a lot of them that were 20's and 30's, too; that were drafted but were all put together. So it was tough.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Hard to --

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: And then they discipline you and, you know, like, you know, they feel your face and say what's this? It's nothing. He said, "Yeah. You got a lot of peach fuzz. I want to see that off tomorrow." So then I had to start shaving. I didn't shave when I went in. So I had to go down and buy a razor and stuff and start shaving because they wanted clean shaving and this and that.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Yeah. Was it like what you expected, do you think?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. It was and I wouldn't trade it for anything. It was great. I saw a lot of the world and it was a good experience and I came back in one piece.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Definitely good thing, right there.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: So you were on a ship then or --

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah, most of the time I was -- let's see -- yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Would you --

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Well, I had. I was on -- three ships. One was a tanker. We carried crude oil and high octane gasoline to the islands in the Pacific and we went and shuttled from San Francisco -- from L.A. to San Francisco to the Marshall Islands in the South Pacific and Hawaiian Islands and then we went to Panama and then we went back and then we went back to Panama and then they took me off at Panama and I was on Base Air for a month and they put me on a C-2 cargo ship; which was a ship going from France to Japan for the war with Japan. And they were moving Army trucks and stuff and they were on the ship I was on. It was a big cargo ship. And then the last one I was on was a garbage gaul (?) in Long Beach Harbor.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Okay. And the -- the ships were civilian ships that you were --

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: No, they were-- Yeah. They were civilian ships -- they were U.S. Merchant Marines. Which was -- they were privately owned, they belonged to the Merchant Marine but they were privately companies but they had Navy armed guards on them to protect them. We had -- they had mounted guns and we were on the ships as gunners.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: All right, so they were like cargo ships with --

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah. With a Navy crew of seventeen men and we manned .20 millimeter-three-inch and five-inch guns, front and back, front and starboard and fantail and then we had four .20 millimeter gun tote around the back, so --

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: So, what job -- were you under, what was your position?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: That was called armed guard, armed guard. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: So the you were with that position then was called?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: I was a gunner but I was just a Seaman First Class. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Seaman First Class?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: All right and in the -- in the typhoon that occurred?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Around that time?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: That was around 1945.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: 1945. The end of war?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah. Pretty much we were waiting out in the Sea of Japan off of Okinawa and there were five hundred ships waiting in there for the invasion of Japan and we were just sitting off of Okinawa Island and this typhoon came in and they said everybody scatter. So everybody -- all the ships just took off. A lot of them were smaller ships than ours and they sank. And it was, oh, a hundred and fifty, two hundred mile hour winds, you know. And you could look out the porthole and see these ships sinking. And you could hear, "Mayday, mayday, SOS, SOS." And you couldn't do anything. You just -- we thought our ship was going down too and it cracked. Yeah, I thought it was going to sink because we were sitting there in what we call passageway which is like a hallway. I had my feet against one wall, my back against the other and we were rolling. You know, and you could hear and we were just rolling. And it was way other here and then it cracked and then it slowly came back up and when we got to New York they checked it and they said it was a big crack in there but it took on a little water but it wasn't bad --

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: -- they just closed off that section down at the bottom of that ship and we made it but --

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: But boy all the jeeps and trucks were hanging over the side of ships that were on top and on the deck, you know.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: The cables had just been ripped off and it was a mess. But it was -- was an experience because I saw all these people in the water drowning and there wasn't anybody that could help them.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: I understand.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: It was scary.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: So was there anything you guys could do like during the typhoon or were you told to go down to like your quarters and like protect yourselves or did you guys have to do any bridge duty or anything?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: No, they wouldn't. They sealed up the whole ship and you had to just stay put. The guys got hungry. We were like that way for four days and four nights. And the guys got hungry --

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: -- and went into the mess hall and started open up cabinets well every time the ship would roll all the dishes would come out. We had the biggest mess. So they just made you sit put and not do anything until it was over with.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Get real seasick?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah. I was lucky I didn't. I never did get seasick. That first -- when -- in boot camp when we went on first cruise, why, they gave us a coffee can, you know, and I told the guy I don't need this I never got sick in my life. So he made me clean up everybody else's puke and I never got sick but I, you know, I still -- I said I don't need it and I didn't. I never did. Any of it. I think it's a mind thing, you know.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Yeah, mostly is. People think they're going to get seasick and they do a little bit.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Because we were on a fishing boat some years ago and everybody got sick.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Everybody and I never did but I just sat there and my -- my youngest son with us and he kind of got squeamish and he said you watch all these over people puking and you just want to do it too.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Yeah, gets to you?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Gets to you. Its a contagious thing.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Definitely?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Were there any other big memorable events that you can think of?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Well, everything -- everything was really important to me cause I was so young and I was seeing different places. But the typhoon and then when we went back after the war our ship was the main base was New York City. So we went through the Panama Canal and up the Atlantic Coast into New York and Manhattan and I got to go ashore and go to New York and have "Liberty" before we came back to California.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: We caught a train and came back to California on the Liberty.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: So when you were out on sea, how long was each of your deployments on each of the ships you were on?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Well, the first year was about a year and then the second time was about a year.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Well, on one ship?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah, on one ship and then the other ship. Yeah. They were about equal space.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Equal?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: So you were in for two years then?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Two years. Yeah. Or pretty close to it. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Then that was around the time with the -- before the -- they wanted to have the invasion with Japan that had been --

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: We signed the treaty on the ship out there in the Pacific and it was all over with, you know. So nobody had the invasion of Japan or nobody went to it, you know, so.

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Do you have any pictures or any like notes or anything from when you were on the ship or journals or anything you might want the share?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: I don't.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: No. All right. That's fine. We were just curious in case you wanted to?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: No. You know, most of that stuff got lost in the moves and stuff, you know, and I don't have anything. I don't think I have anything.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: That's fine, yeah. Just in case?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Karl Arnet
sp.p: Well, thank you thank you very much?

sp.speaker: Ellis Barklow
sp.p: Glad to do it.
